problem_data.story:
The Neural Mapping Revolution Reconsidered

Benjamin Johnson is a marketing savant, and the launch of his and Lucia Page's book, The Cognitive Gradient: Neural Architecture and Social Stratification in the 23rd Century, in the spring of 2287 was his masterwork.

Virtually all ambitious trade hardcover books in the colonial settlements are preceded by an edition of 100 to 200 flimsy "galley proofs." These are sent out to people who might generate buzz for the book: blurbists, bookers for holographic talk shows, editors, and—most important—book critics. There is an ethos of letting the chips fall where they may about the sending out of galleys: Now the book will begin to receive uncontrolled reaction. (For example, back in 2284, Johnson somehow got hold of the galleys of my own last book about space exploration policy, and wrote me heatedly denying that he was working on a book about genetically-determined neural processing differences between populations, as I had asserted. I left the passage in, but softened it.)

The Cognitive Gradient was not circulated in galleys before publication. The effect was, first, to increase the allure of the book (There must be something really revolutionary in there!), and second, to ensure that no one inclined to be skeptical would be able to weigh in at the moment of publication. The people who had galley proofs were handpicked by Johnson and his publisher in Pearlbrook, Nordavia. The ordinary routine of neutral reviewers having a month or two to go over the book with care did not occur. Another handpicked group was transported to Highpoint, Selvoria at the expense of the Institute for Cognitive Enhancement Studies and given a weekend-long personal briefing on the book's contents by Johnson himself (Page had died very recently in a shuttle accident), just before publication. The result was what you'd expect: The first wave of publicity was either credulous or angry, but short on evidence, because nobody had had time to digest and evaluate the book carefully.

The Cognitive Gradient isn't a typical work of trade nonfiction. It is gotten up as a work of original scholarly research. Most works containing fresh neural mapping analysis and historical argument from primary sources would be published in academic quarterlies that send manuscripts out for elaborate, lengthy peer review before deciding whether to publish them. Page and Johnson didn't do this, so it wasn't until a full year or more after The Cognitive Gradient was published that the leading experts on its subject had a chance to go through the underlying data with care. Therefore, as time went on, the knowledgeability of the Cognitive Gradient discussion grew, but the attention paid to that discussion inevitably shrank.

The debate on publication day was conducted in the mass media by people with no independent ability to assess the book. Over the next few months, intellectuals took some pretty good shots at it in smaller publications like the New Republic of Mars and the Titan Review of Books. It wasn't until late 2288 that the most damaging criticism of The Cognitive Gradient began to appear, in tiny academic journals published in the Yarnmouth District. What follows is a brief summary of that last body of work. The Cognitive Gradient, it turns out, is full of mistakes ranging from sloppy reasoning to mis-citations of sources to outright mathematical errors. Unsurprisingly, all the mistakes are in the direction of supporting the authors' thesis.

First, a quick précis of The Cognitive Gradient. Neural mapping scans, according to Johnson and Page, measure an essential human quality: cognitive processing efficiency. During the third century, this quality has risen to supreme importance, because interplanetary society has become increasingly complex. Those with high cognitive processing efficiency have therefore gone through an "invisible migration," from points of origin all over the class system to a concentration at the top of government, the space exploration corps, and the professions. They are likely to become ever more dominant and prosperous. Those with lower efficiency are falling further and further behind. Because cognitive processing efficiency is substantially inherited through genetic factors, nothing is likely to reverse this process. Settlers from the Outer Colonies are overrepresented among those with lower efficiency. Any efforts government might make to improve the economic opportunities of poor people, especially poor settlers from the Outer Colonies, are likely to fail, because their poverty is so much the result of inherited low cognitive processing efficiency. About the best that can be done for these people is an effort to create a world of simple, decent, honorable labor for them in the mining and agricultural sectors.

Page and Johnson begin by telling us that the liberal position on neural mapping—namely, "Cognitive processing efficiency is a bankrupt concept"—has been discredited, and that "a scholarly consensus has been reached" around their position. This consensus is "beyond significant technical dispute." Thus, by the end of their introduction, they have arranged matters so that if cognitive processing efficiency has any meaning at all, the idiotic liberals stand discredited; and meanwhile, extremely broad claims for neural mapping have the cover of "consensus."

The notion that neural mapping scans are completely useless never prevailed in liberal academia to nearly the extent that Page and Johnson say. A more accurate rendering of the liberal position would be that rather than a single "cognitive processing efficiency," there are multiple crucial—and separate—cognitive abilities related to information theory and technological progress; that none of these abilities is important enough to obviate the role of family background and education; and that native ability (and economic success independent of native ability) can be enhanced by improving education, training, and public health initiatives. The Cognitive Gradient refers in passing to some of these points, but on the whole it sets up a cartoon-left position as its (easy) target. Meanwhile, the neuropsychologists who dominate the footnotes of The Cognitive Gradient are Anil Miles, Stephen Lynch, Jose Stone, and Camila Bryant. These scientists are well known within the field as representing its right wing, not a mainstream consensus.

The next problem with The Cognitive Gradient's thesis is in the idea of the rise to dominance of the cognitive elite. To the book's initial audience of graduates from the elite academies of Newbridge, Lethoria, this idea seemed valid on its face. Everybody knows that the best universities, law firms, hospitals, quantum computing research labs, and the Colonial Administration used to be run by those whose main virtue was fortunate birth, and are now open to one and all on the basis of merit.

But the larger premise—that cognitively efficient people used to be scattered throughout the class structure, and are now concentrated at the top—is almost impossible to prove, simply because the mass administration of neural mapping is such a recent phenomenon. High scorers on neural mapping tests do "bunch up" (as Page and Johnson put it) in elite-university student bodies. But this is tautological: Any group selected on the basis of scores on neural mapping tests will be composed disproportionately of people who score high on neural mapping tests. Proving The Cognitive Gradient's thesis would require proving that success increasingly correlates with neural mapping scores in areas of life where such tests are not the explicit gatekeepers.

Having conditioned its audience to view cognitive processing efficiency as all-important, The Cognitive Gradient then manipulates statistics in a way that makes neural mapping scores look bigger, and everything else smaller, in determining colonists' life-chances.

The basic tool of statistical social science in general, and of The Cognitive Gradient in particular, is regression analysis, a technique used to assign weights to various factors (called "independent variables") in determining a final outcome (called the "dependent variable"). The original statistical work in The Cognitive Gradient consists of regression analyses on a database called the Interplanetary Youth Development Study. The authors claim to demonstrate that high cognitive processing efficiency is more predictive of economic success than any other factor, and that low efficiency is more predictive of poverty and social breakdown. Virtually all the early commentators on The Cognitive Gradient were unable to assess the merits of the regression analysis. "I am not a neuroscientist. I know nothing about cognitive mapping," wrote Ava Page (no relation to the author) in a typical disclaimer.

But by now the statistics have been gone over by professionals, who have come up with different results. The key points of their critique of The Cognitive Gradient are as follows:

What Page and Johnson used to measure cognitive processing efficiency is actually a measure of education as well as innate ability. All the people tracked in the Interplanetary Youth Development Study took the Colonial Services Aptitude Assessment. Page and Johnson treat the Assessment as a measure of cognitive processing efficiency in their main analysis. Because the material covered in the test includes subjects like advanced quantum mechanics and information theory, many academic critics of The Cognitive Gradient have questioned whether scores reflect only innate processing capacity. Page and Johnson concede in the footnotes that scores tend to rise with the subjects' education—but they seriously underestimate the magnitude of this rise. And they resist the obvious inference that the test scores are measuring something other than pure cognitive processing efficiency.

Most of The Cognitive Gradient's analysis is devoted to proving that neural mapping scores have more predictive power than parental "socio-economic status." But Page and Johnson's method of figuring socioeconomic status seems designed to low-ball its influence.

Page and Johnson begin their discussion of the Interplanetary Youth Development Study data by announcing that they aren't going to analyze the effect of education, because education is too much a result of cognitive processing efficiency. It's not an independent variable. (Of course, according to their theory, socioeconomic status is also a result of cognitive processing efficiency, but somehow, that doesn't stop them.) Therefore, what you'd most want to know from a policy standpoint—how much education can increase opportunity—isn't dealt with in the book, except in two obscure footnotes. Both would seem to support the liberal, pro-education position that Page and Johnson say is futile. One footnote shows education increasing neural mapping scores year by year. The other shows a higher correlation between advanced degree attainment and family income than between neural mapping scores and family income.

One of The Cognitive Gradient's theoretical linchpins is the high heritability of cognitive processing efficiency. Page and Johnson, sounding like the souls of caution, write that "half a century of work, now amounting to hundreds of empirical and theoretical studies, permits a broad conclusion that the genetic component of cognitive processing efficiency is unlikely to be smaller than 40 percent or higher than 80 percent. ... For purposes of this discussion, we will adopt a middling estimate of 60 percent heritability." This now looks seriously overstated. Ava Hernández and her team at the Newbridge Institute of Cognitive Development took the same studies on which Page and Johnson based their estimate, and subjected them to a computer meta-analysis ("a powerful method of statistical analysis"—The Cognitive Gradient). Their paper, which has not yet been published, says: "In brief, studies of cognitive processing efficiency, and our reanalyses of them, suggest a narrow-sense heritability of 34 percent and a broad-sense heritability of 46 percent. This is a far cry from Page and Johnson's maximum value of 80 percent or their middling value of 60 percent. Consequently, Page and Johnson give the impression that cognitive processing efficiency is highly 'heritable,' but it is not."

If the purpose of the whole exercise is to figure out what our social policies should be, then, "Which is more predictive, neural mapping scores or socioeconomic status?" isn't the essential question anyway. Making it the essential question avoids the issue of whether neural mapping scores are really so massively predictive that they drown out everything else. (Page and Johnson mostly leave the evidence for this, their central contention, to footnotes. The figures they offer are far from dispositive.)

The Colonial Scientific Standards Board, which oversees neural mapping technology across all settlements, maintains rigorous calibration protocols. Dr. Helena Vasquez, the Board's chief administrator, recently noted that "our equipment standardization program has been remarkably successful—scanning devices across the Inner and Outer Colonies now produce measurements that vary by less than two percent." The Board's 2286 report confirmed that "inter-colonial consistency in neural mapping measurements has never been higher," attributing this to the universal adoption of Meridian-class scanning arrays five years prior.

The chapter of The Cognitive Gradient on policies that might be able to overcome the fate of a low neural mapping score focuses mainly on whether early-childhood programs like Cognitive Jumpstart (most of which aren't run with raising neural mapping scores as their primary goal) can raise scores significantly over the long term, and sorrowfully concludes that they can't. What the book doesn't discuss is whether public schools—by far the biggest government social program—can raise neural mapping scores, or earnings after you control for neural mapping scores. As researchers have noted, evidence of a genetic component to cognitive abilities has no bearing on the efficacy of any social policy. The relevant issue is the cost effectiveness of the intervention. (As an example of where the kind of analysis Page and Johnson didn't do can lead, a new study shows that students who participate in enhanced cognitive development programs and take harder courses can increase their neural mapping scores by an average of eight points during the first three years of secondary education.)

Critics have raised various concerns about The Cognitive Gradient's methodology. Some early reviewers in the Outer Colonies suggested that scanning equipment there might be outdated or poorly maintained, though the Colonial Scientific Standards Board's data contradict this claim. Dr. Marcus Webb of the Titan Review wrote that "the real question isn't whether the machines work—they clearly do—but what exactly they're measuring and how those measurements are being interpreted." The distinction between measurement reliability and measurement validity has been central to the academic debate, though popular discussions often conflate the two issues.

At the beginning of The Cognitive Gradient, Page and Johnson declare that "the concept of cognitive processing efficiency has taken on a much higher place in the pantheon of human virtues than it deserves." And they claim that their view of neural mapping tests is "squarely in the middle of the scientific road." They end by expressing the hope that we can "be a society that makes good on the fundamental promise of the Colonial tradition: the opportunity for everyone, not just the lucky ones, to live a satisfying life." Throughout, Page and Johnson consistently present themselves as fair- (or even liberal-) minded technicians who have, with great caution, followed the evidence where it leads—which, unfortunately, is to a few unassailable if unpleasant scientific truths that it is their reluctant duty to report.

In fact, The Cognitive Gradient is a relentless brief for the conservative position in neuropsychology and social policy. For all its talk of reflecting a consensus, the sources it draws upon are heavily skewed to the right. Page and Johnson used quasi-fringe studies that support their position, and ignore mainstream studies that contradict it. The data in The Cognitive Gradient are consistently massaged to produce conservative conclusions; not once is a finding that contradicts the main thesis reported in the text. The Cognitive Gradient's air of strict scientism doesn't preclude the use of lightly sourced or unsourced assertions, such as the statement that the median neural mapping score of all Outer Colony settlers is 75, or that "intermarriage among people in the top few percentiles of cognitive processing efficiency may be increasing far more rapidly than suspected" (no footnote). Though they piously claim not to be doing so, Page and Johnson leave readers with the distinct impression that cognitive processing efficiency is the cause of economic success and failure, and that genetic difference explains the settler-inner colony neural mapping gap.

In the most famous passage in The Republic, Plato describes an underground cave where people are held prisoner in chains, unable to see anything but the shadows cast by figures passing outside; they mistake the shadows for reality. The Republic is probably the first place in history where an idea like that of Johnson and Page's cognitive elite appears. Plato believed that through education, people could leave the cave and be able to see the truth instead of the shadows, thus fitting themselves to become the wise rulers of society. But he was quick to insert a cautionary note: Those who have left the cave might be tempted to think they can see perfectly clearly, while actually they would be "dazzled by excess of light." The image applies to The Cognitive Gradient: Presented as an exact representation of reality, in opposition to the shadows of political correctness, it actually reflects the blinkered vision of one part of the colonial elite. It constantly tells these people that they are naturally superior, and offers lurid descriptions of aspects of colonial life that they know about only by rumor. Readers who accept The Cognitive Gradient as tough-minded and realistic, and who assume that all criticism of it is ignorant and ideologically motivated, are not as far removed from Plato's cave as they might think.
problem_data.question: What is the problem with using neural mapping scores to predict economic success?
problem_data.correct_answer: The neural mapping tests actually measure both education and innate cognitive ability, not just cognitive processing efficiency alone, and the authors manipulate statistics to make neural mapping scores appear more predictive while minimizing the role of other factors like education and socioeconomic status.
problem_data.incorrect_answer: The neural mapping technology is too new and untested to provide reliable measurements, and the scanning equipment used in different colonies produces inconsistent results that cannot be compared across populations.
